source.text: ט֥וֹב שֵׁ֖ם מִשֶּׁ֣מֶן ט֑וֹב וְי֣וֹם הַמָּ֔וֶת מִיּ֖וֹם הִוָּלְדֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: Better a name than oil good, and [the] day of the death than [the] day of his being born.

en.L: Better [is] a name than good oil, \q and the day of death than the day of {{gender:one's|his}} birth.
en.B: A good name is worth more than fine perfume, \q and the day of death more than the day of birth.
en.R: A good reputation is worth more than costly perfume. \q And the day a person dies is better than the day they were born.

decisions.choice: a name ... oil: a play on two words that sound alike
decisions.reason: The word for "name" (*shem*) and the word for "oil" (*shemen*) sound almost the same. The saying begins the cluster of "better than" proverbs that runs through verse 14, and the sound play makes it easy to remember.

decisions.choice: a name: a good reputation
decisions.reason: As in Proverbs 22:1, a "name" is what others know and say about a person. The word "good" stands in the second half of the line in the Hebrew, so it belongs to both: a good name is better than good oil.

decisions.choice: the day of death is better than the day of birth: only at death is a life complete
decisions.reason: Scented oil was a luxury that soon wore off. A name lasts. The day of birth is all promise, but at death a life and its name are finished and can be weighed (verse 8). The saying is sober rather than despairing; in 9:4 the same book says that a living dog is better than a dead lion. The book lets such sayings stand side by side (see 1:2).

decisions.choice: good oil: fine scented oil
decisions.reason: Olive oil mixed with spices was rubbed on the skin and hair at feasts and on special days (9:8; Psalm 133:2). Good oil was costly and pleasant, and its scent spread through a house (Song of Songs 1:3).

decisions.choice: fine perfume (B); costly perfume (R)
decisions.reason: The oil meant here is the scented oil of feasts (m4), which most readers now know as perfume. Literal keeps "good oil" so that the sound play with "name" (m1) can be seen.

decisions.choice: the day a person dies ... the day they were born
decisions.reason: Readable makes the person explicit. Literal keeps the Hebrew "his" (meaning anyone) with the gender setting.

source.text: ט֞וֹב לָלֶ֣כֶת אֶל־בֵּֽית־אֵ֗בֶל מִלֶּ֨כֶת֙ אֶל־בֵּ֣ית מִשְׁתֶּ֔ה בַּאֲשֶׁ֕ר ה֖וּא ס֣וֹף כָּל־הָאָדָ֑ם וְהַחַ֖י יִתֵּ֥ן אֶל־לִבּֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: Better to go to [a] house of mourning than to go to [a] house of feasting, in that it [is the] end of all humankind, and the living will give [it] to his heart.

en.L: Better to go to a house of mourning than to go to a house of feasting, \q because that [is] the end of every human, \q and the living will lay [it] to heart.
en.B: It is better to go to a house of mourning \q than to go to a house of feasting, \q because death is the end of everyone, \q and the living will take it to heart.
en.R: It is better to go where people are mourning a death \q than to go where people are having a party. \q Everyone dies in the end, \q and those who are still alive will think about that.

decisions.choice: a house of mourning: a home where a death is being mourned; a house of feasting: a house where a drinking feast is held
decisions.reason: After a death the family mourned at home for several days, and friends came to sit and grieve with them (Genesis 50:10; Job 2:13). The word for "feasting" comes from the verb "to drink": a banquet with wine (Esther 1:5; Jeremiah 16:8, where the two kinds of house are also set side by side).

decisions.choice: that is the end of every human: death, which the house of mourning brings to mind
alternatives: that is the end of the matter for everyone
decisions.reason: "That" points to what the house of mourning is about: death, which comes to everyone (3:19-20; 9:2-3).

decisions.choice: will lay it to heart: will think seriously about it
decisions.reason: To "give" something "to the heart" is to take it in and think about it (9:1). The verb can be read as a plain future, "will", or as what ought to happen, "should". Either way the point is that a funeral makes the living think about their own end.

decisions.choice: death
decisions.reason: Balanced names what "that" refers to (m2); Literal keeps the pronoun.

decisions.choice: having a party
decisions.reason: Readable uses an everyday word for a drinking feast (m1).

source.text: ט֥וֹב כַּ֖עַס מִשְּׂחֹ֑ק כִּֽי־בְרֹ֥עַ פָּנִ֖ים יִ֥יטַב לֵֽב׃

records.literal_gloss: Better grief than laughter, for in sadness of face is made good [the] heart.

en.L: Better [is] grief than laughter, \q for in sadness of face the heart is made good.
en.B: Grief is better than laughter, \q for a sad face can be good for the heart.
en.R: Sorrow is better than laughter, \q because a sad face can do the heart good.

decisions.choice: grief: sorrow, being troubled
decisions.reason: The word (*ka'as*) can mean anger, irritation or grief (1:18; 2:23). Set against laughter here, it is grief. In verse 9 the same word is anger. The book uses it both ways in a few lines.

decisions.choice: the heart is made good: the inner person becomes better, wiser
alternatives: the heart may be glad (though the face is sad)
decisions.reason: The verb means to be good or to be made good. It can mean being glad (Judges 19:6), and some read: "though the face is sad, the heart may be happy." In this cluster of sayings, which prize the house of mourning (verses 2 and 4), the likelier sense is that sorrow does a person good: it makes the heart wiser.

decisions.choice: grief better than laughter: a saying that stands against the book's call to enjoy life
decisions.reason: Elsewhere the book tells its readers to eat their bread with joy (9:7) and calls laughter madness (2:2). Here grief is better than laughter. The book sets these sayings against each other, and the translation does not smooth them (see 1:2).

decisions.choice: can be good for the heart (B); can do the heart good (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable keep the general word "good", which can carry both senses in m2, and add "can" because the saying states what sorrow is able to do, not what it always does.

source.text: לֵ֤ב חֲכָמִים֙ בְּבֵ֣ית אֵ֔בֶל וְלֵ֥ב כְּסִילִ֖ים בְּבֵ֥ית שִׂמְחָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: [The] heart of [the] wise [is] in [the] house of mourning, and [the] heart of fools [is] in [the] house of pleasure.

en.L: The heart of [the] wise [is] in a house of mourning, \q but the heart of fools [is] in a house of gladness.
en.B: The hearts of the wise are in the house of mourning, \q but the hearts of fools are in the house of pleasure.
en.R: Wise people think about the house where people mourn. \q Foolish people think only about the house where people have fun.

decisions.choice: the heart is in: the thoughts and desires turn to
decisions.reason: In Hebrew the heart is the seat of thought and will as well as feeling. The wise give their minds to the lesson of the house of mourning (verse 2); fools want only the house of pleasure.

decisions.choice: fools: people who are dull and pleased with themselves
decisions.reason: This word for fool (*kesil*) is the one Proverbs uses for the self-satisfied person who does not want understanding (Proverbs 1:22; 18:2). In Ecclesiastes it stands for the opposite of the wise (2:14-16; 4:5).

decisions.choice: fools (L, B); foolish people (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide wording for *kesil*: "fool" at Literal and Balanced, "foolish person" ("foolish people") at Readable, which keeps the word from sounding like a playground insult.

decisions.choice: think about ... think only about
decisions.reason: Readable says what "the heart is in" means (m1). "Only" draws out the contrast between the two halves of the line.

source.text: ט֕וֹב לִשְׁמֹ֖עַ גַּעֲרַ֣ת חָכָ֑ם מֵאִ֕ישׁ שֹׁמֵ֖עַ שִׁ֥יר כְּסִילִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: Better to hear [the] rebuke of [a] wise [one] than [for a] man [to be] hearing [the] song of fools.

en.L: Better to listen to the rebuke of a wise [one] \q than for {{gender:a person|a man}} to listen to the song of fools.
en.B: It is better to listen to a wise person's rebuke \q than to listen to the song of fools.
en.R: It is better to let a wise person correct you \q than to listen to foolish people singing.

decisions.choice: rebuke: a sharp warning or correction
decisions.reason: The word is used for a stern word that stops someone (Proverbs 13:1; 17:10). It is unpleasant to hear, but it does good.

decisions.choice: the song of fools: the singing at their feasts, and perhaps their flattering praise
decisions.reason: The song belongs to the house of pleasure of verse 4. Set against a wise person's rebuke, it may also mean the pleasant words of fools who tell people only what they want to hear. Either way, it is pleasant and useless.

decisions.choice: fools (L, B); foolish people (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide wording for *kesil*: "fool" at Literal and Balanced, "foolish person" ("foolish people") at Readable, which keeps the word from sounding like a playground insult.

decisions.choice: (no word for "a man")
alternatives: than for a man to listen
decisions.reason: The Hebrew names a man as the one who listens to the song; it means anyone. Balanced and Readable leave the word out, since "it is better to listen" already speaks of anyone. Literal keeps it with the gender setting.

source.text: כִּ֣י כְק֤וֹל הַסִּירִים֙ תַּ֣חַת הַסִּ֔יר כֵּ֖ן שְׂחֹ֣ק הַכְּסִ֑יל וְגַם־זֶ֖ה הָֽבֶל׃

records.literal_gloss: For like [the] crackling of the thorns under the pot, so [is the] laughter of the fool; and also this [is] breath.

en.L: For like the crackling of the thorns under the pot, \q so [is] the laughter of the fool; \q and this too [is] breath.
en.B: For like thorns crackling under a pot \q is the laughter of a fool. \q This too is a breath.
en.R: When a foolish person laughs, it is like thorns crackling under a cooking pot: \q a lot of noise that is quickly gone. \q This too is only a breath.

decisions.choice: the thorns under the pot: a play on two words that sound alike
decisions.reason: The word for "thorns" (*sirim*) and the word for "pot" (*sir*) sound almost the same, like the sound play in verse 1. The noisy laughter of fools is heard in the sound of the line.

decisions.choice: thorns under the pot: dry brush used as fuel, which blazes up noisily and burns out at once
decisions.reason: Dry thornbushes were a common fuel for cooking (Psalm 58:10). They catch quickly, crackle loudly and are gone before the pot is properly heated (Psalm 118:12). So is the laughter of a fool: loud and soon over.

decisions.choice: breath: short-lived and empty
decisions.reason: The book's key word (*hevel*), a breath or vapor (see the main note at 1:2). Here the sense leans toward what is brief and without substance, like the flash of burning thorns.

decisions.choice: this too: the fool's laughter
decisions.reason: "This too" most naturally points to what has just been described, the laughter of fools. Some take it to cover the whole comparison between the wise and fools, as in 2:15.

decisions.choice: breath (L); a breath (B); only a breath (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide wording for *hevel*, which keeps the picture of breath at every level (see 1:2). Readable has already said what the picture means here (r-en-2), so it keeps the plain picture.

decisions.choice: a lot of noise that is quickly gone
decisions.reason: Readable spells out the point of the image (m2), which readers who have never cooked over a fire of thorns could miss. The line adds no new idea to the Hebrew picture.

decisions.choice: the fool (L); a fool (B); a foolish person (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide wording for *kesil*: "fool" at Literal and Balanced, "foolish person" ("foolish people") at Readable, which keeps the word from sounding like a playground insult.

source.text: כִּ֥י הָעֹ֖שֶׁק יְהוֹלֵ֣ל חָכָ֑ם וִֽיאַבֵּ֥ד אֶת־לֵ֖ב מַתָּנָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: For the oppression makes mad [a] wise [one], and destroys the heart [a] gift.

en.L: Surely oppression makes a wise [one] mad, \q and a gift destroys the heart.
en.B: Oppression can drive a wise person mad, \q and a bribe corrupts the heart.
en.R: Oppression can make even a wise person act like a fool. \q And a bribe can ruin a person's mind.

decisions.choice: oppression: wrong done by force, most likely gain squeezed out of others
decisions.reason: The word (*'osheq*) means oppression or extortion (4:1; 5:7). It is not clear whether the wise person suffers it or practices it. Set beside the bribe, it may mean gain taken by force: getting rich at others' expense ruins a wise person's judgment. Others read that being crushed by oppression drives even the wise to madness. The renderings keep both open.

decisions.choice: makes mad: makes a person act like a fool
decisions.reason: The verb is from the same root as "madness" (1:17; 2:12; 7:25). It describes someone who has lost good sense.

decisions.choice: a gift destroys the heart: a bribe corrupts judgment
decisions.reason: The law says that a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise (Exodus 23:8; Deuteronomy 16:19), and Proverbs warns against it (Proverbs 15:27; 17:23). Here the heart, the seat of understanding (verse 4), is destroyed by it.

decisions.choice: surely: the line is joined loosely to what comes before
decisions.reason: The verse begins with a small word that often means "for". It is hard to see how this saying explains verse 6, so it is taken here as "surely", marking a new saying in the cluster.

decisions.choice: a bribe
decisions.reason: The word means a gift, but a gift that destroys the heart is a bribe (m3). Literal keeps "gift".

decisions.choice: a person's mind
decisions.reason: Readable says "mind" because here the heart is a person's power to judge rightly (m3).

source.text: ט֛וֹב אַחֲרִ֥ית דָּבָ֖ר מֵֽרֵאשִׁית֑וֹ ט֥וֹב אֶֽרֶךְ־ר֖וּחַ מִגְּבַהּ־רֽוּחַ׃

records.literal_gloss: Better [the] end of [a] matter than its beginning; better [the one] long of spirit than [the one] high of spirit.

en.L: Better [is the] end of a matter than its beginning; \q better [is one who is] long of spirit than [one who is] high of spirit.
en.B: The end of a matter is better than its beginning, \q and patience is better than pride.
en.R: The end of something is better than its beginning. \q Being patient is better than being proud.

decisions.choice: the end of a matter: how a thing turns out
decisions.reason: The word (*davar*) can mean a word or a matter. A thing can only be judged when it is finished, as a life is only complete at death (verse 1).

decisions.choice: long of spirit: patient; high of spirit: proud
decisions.reason: A "long" spirit is slow to anger and willing to wait (Proverbs 14:29, where a similar phrase is used). A "high" spirit is arrogant (Proverbs 16:18). The patient person waits to see how things end; the proud person does not.

decisions.choice: patience ... pride (B); being patient ... being proud (R)
alternatives: the long of spirit ... the high of spirit
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the two idioms mean (m2). Literal keeps the Hebrew pictures.

source.text: אַל־תְּבַהֵ֥ל בְּרֽוּחֲךָ֖ לִכְע֑וֹס כִּ֣י כַ֔עַס בְּחֵ֥יק כְּסִילִ֖ים יָנֽוּחַ׃

records.literal_gloss: Do not be hasty in your spirit to be angry, for anger in [the] bosom of fools rests.

en.L: Do not be hasty in your spirit to grow angry, \q for anger lodges in the bosom of fools.
en.B: Do not let your spirit be quick to anger, \q for anger makes its home in the heart of fools.
en.R: Do not be quick to get angry. \q Anger lives in the hearts of foolish people.

decisions.choice: anger: irritation that flares up
decisions.reason: This is the same word (*ka'as*) that means "grief" in verse 3. Here, with "hasty", it is quick anger, as in Proverbs 12:16.

decisions.choice: rests in the bosom: settles in and stays
decisions.reason: The bosom is the chest, where something precious is kept close (Proverbs 6:27). Anger finds a home in the fool and settles there, as wisdom rests in the heart of the wise (Proverbs 14:33).

decisions.choice: heart (B); hearts (R)
decisions.reason: "Bosom" is now old-fashioned. Balanced and Readable use "heart", the inner person; Literal keeps the Hebrew word.

decisions.choice: fools (L, B); foolish people (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide wording for *kesil*: "fool" at Literal and Balanced, "foolish person" ("foolish people") at Readable, which keeps the word from sounding like a playground insult.

source.text: אַל־תֹּאמַר֙ מֶ֣ה הָיָ֔ה שֶׁ֤הַיָּמִים֙ הָרִ֣אשֹׁנִ֔ים הָי֥וּ טוֹבִ֖ים מֵאֵ֑לֶּה כִּ֛י לֹ֥א מֵחָכְמָ֖ה שָׁאַ֥לְתָּ עַל־זֶֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Do not say, What was [it] that the days the former were better than these? for not from wisdom you ask about this.

en.L: Do not say, "How [is it] that the former days were better than these?" \q for not from wisdom do you ask about this.
en.B: Do not say, "How is it that earlier days were better than these?" \q It is not wisdom that prompts that question.
en.R: Do not ask, "Why were things better in the old days?" \q It is not wise to ask that.

decisions.choice: not from wisdom: the question does not come from wisdom
alternatives: you do not ask wisely about this
decisions.reason: The question takes for granted that the past was better. Asking it comes from discontent, not from wisdom.

decisions.choice: the former days were not better: every age has the same troubles
decisions.reason: The book has already said that there is nothing new under the sun and that what has been will be again (1:9-11; 3:15). Longing for a golden age misreads the way things are.

decisions.choice: double quotation marks for the question
decisions.reason: Qoheleth's own voice takes no quotation marks; words he quotes inside it take double quotation marks.

source.text: טוֹבָ֥ה חָכְמָ֖ה עִֽם־נַחֲלָ֑ה וְיֹתֵ֖ר לְרֹאֵ֥י הַשָּֽׁמֶשׁ׃

records.literal_gloss: Good [is] wisdom with an inheritance, and an advantage to those seeing the sun.

en.L: Good [is] wisdom with an inheritance, \q and an advantage to those who see the sun.
en.B: Wisdom is good along with an inheritance, \q and an advantage to those who see the sun.
en.R: Wisdom is good to have along with an inheritance. \q It is a help to everyone who is alive.

decisions.choice: with an inheritance: wisdom together with wealth
decisions.reason: The small word means "with". Some take it as a comparison, "wisdom is as good as an inheritance", which suits verse 12. Read as "with", the saying is that wisdom is good and that it is better still with the means to live. Both readings set wisdom beside money, as verse 12 does.

decisions.choice: those who see the sun: the living
decisions.reason: To see the sun is to be alive (6:5; 11:7; Psalm 58:9).

decisions.choice: advantage: what is more, what a person gains
decisions.reason: The word (*yoter*) is related to *yitron*, "gain" (see 1:3), and means what is left over, an advantage (6:8, 11). Wisdom brings a real benefit in this life.

decisions.choice: everyone who is alive
decisions.reason: Readable says what the idiom means (m2).

source.text: כִּ֛י בְּצֵ֥ל הַֽחָכְמָ֖ה בְּצֵ֣ל הַכָּ֑סֶף וְיִתְר֣וֹן דַּ֔עַת הַֽחָכְמָ֖ה תְּחַיֶּ֥ה בְעָלֶֽיהָ׃

records.literal_gloss: For in [the] shade of the wisdom, in [the] shade of the silver; and [the] gain of knowledge: the wisdom gives life to its owners.

en.L: For [to be] in the shade of wisdom [is to be] in the shade of silver, \q but the gain of knowledge [is that] \q wisdom gives life to those who have it.
en.B: For wisdom shelters as money shelters, \q but this is the gain of knowledge: \q wisdom keeps alive those who have it.
en.R: Wisdom protects you, as money protects you. \q But here is the good that knowledge does: \q wisdom keeps alive the people who have it.

decisions.choice: shade: protection
decisions.reason: In a hot land shade is shelter and safety, and "shade" often stands for protection (Psalm 121:5; Isaiah 30:2). Wisdom shelters a person, as money does.

decisions.choice: in the shade of wisdom, in the shade of silver: wisdom protects as money protects
alternatives: one who has wisdom is like one who has money
decisions.reason: The Hebrew sets the two phrases side by side with no verb. The sense is a comparison: the protection of wisdom is like the protection of money. The verse goes on to say where wisdom has the advantage.

decisions.choice: gives life: keeps alive, preserves life
decisions.reason: Money can protect, but it cannot keep a person alive. Wisdom can, as Proverbs says it is a tree of life to those who hold it (Proverbs 3:18; compare Proverbs 13:14).

decisions.choice: money
decisions.reason: Silver was money (5:9). Literal keeps "silver".

decisions.choice: gain (L, B); the good that knowledge does (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide wording for *yitron* (see 1:3): "gain" at Literal and Balanced, "what good it does" at Readable.

source.text: רְאֵ֖ה אֶת־מַעֲשֵׂ֣ה הָאֱלֹהִ֑ים כִּ֣י מִ֤י יוּכַל֙ לְתַקֵּ֔ן אֵ֖ת אֲשֶׁ֥ר עִוְּתֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: See the work of the God, for who is able to make straight what he has bent?

en.L: Look at the work of God, \q for who is able to make straight what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has made crooked?
en.B: Consider what God has done: \q who can straighten what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has made crooked?
en.R: Think about what God has done. \q No one can straighten what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has bent.

decisions.choice: who can straighten what he has made crooked: an echo of 1:15
decisions.reason: In 1:15 Qoheleth says that what is crooked cannot be made straight. Here he says why: it is God who has made it so, and no one can undo God's work (3:14).

decisions.choice: God's work includes what seems crooked to people
decisions.reason: The book does not call God unjust. It says that God's work includes things people cannot understand or change, and that wisdom accepts this (verse 14; 8:17).

decisions.choice: who can ...?: no one can
decisions.reason: The question expects the answer "no one".

decisions.choice: No one can straighten
decisions.reason: Readable states the answer to the question (m3) as a plain sentence.

source.text: בְּי֤וֹם טוֹבָה֙ הֱיֵ֣ה בְט֔וֹב וּבְי֥וֹם רָעָ֖ה רְאֵ֑ה גַּ֣ם אֶת־זֶ֤ה לְעֻמַּת־זֶה֙ עָשָׂ֣ה הָֽאֱלֹהִ֔ים עַל־דִּבְרַ֗ת שֶׁלֹּ֨א יִמְצָ֧א הָֽאָדָ֛ם אַחֲרָ֖יו מְאֽוּמָה׃

records.literal_gloss: In [the] day of good be in good, and in [the] day of evil see; also this alongside this has made the God, on account that not may find the human after him anything.

en.L: In the day of good, be in good, \q and in the day of evil, look: \q God has made the one alongside the other, \q so that {{gender:a person|man}} may not find out anything [that will be] after {{gender:them|him}}.
en.B: When times are good, enjoy the good, \q and when times are bad, consider this: \q God has made the one as well as the other, \q so that no one can find out anything about what is to come.
en.R: When life is good, enjoy it. \q When life is hard, think about this: \q God has made both kinds of days. \q He did it so that no one can know what will happen in the future.

decisions.choice: be in good: enjoy the good
decisions.reason: To "be in good" is to take pleasure in good things while they last (compare 2:24; 3:12-13; 9:7).

decisions.choice: good ... evil: good times and bad times
decisions.reason: The pair means prosperity and misfortune, not right and wrong (*ra'ah* as misfortune, as in 5:12). The same two words describe what God sends in Job 2:10.

decisions.choice: God has made both: good days and bad days alike come from God
decisions.reason: Qoheleth does not explain bad days away. Both kinds come from God's hand, as Job 2:10 and Isaiah 45:7 also say.

decisions.choice: after him: what will come after a person, the future
decisions.reason: The phrase "after him" is used in 3:22 and 6:12 for what will happen after a person, in the future or after death. Because good and bad days alternate in a way no one can predict, no one can know what is coming. Some take "him" as God: no one can find fault with him.

decisions.choice: the day of good ... the day of evil (L); when times are good ... when times are bad (B); when life is good ... when life is hard (R)
alternatives: the day of prosperity ... the day of adversity
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Hebrew pair "good" and "evil" so that the reader can see the repeated word "good". Balanced and Readable say what the pair means here (m2).

decisions.choice: He did it so that
decisions.reason: Readable starts a new sentence for the purpose clause and supplies its subject, God.

source.text: אֶת־הַכֹּ֥ל רָאִ֖יתִי בִּימֵ֣י הֶבְלִ֑י יֵ֤שׁ צַדִּיק֙ אֹבֵ֣ד בְּצִדְק֔וֹ וְיֵ֣שׁ רָשָׁ֔ע מַאֲרִ֖יךְ בְּרָעָתֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: Everything I have seen in [the] days of my breath: there is [a] righteous [one] perishing in his righteousness, and there is [a] wicked [one] prolonging in his evil.

en.L: Everything I have seen in the days of my breath: there is a righteous [person] who perishes in {{gender:their|his}} righteousness, and there is a wicked [person] who prolongs [life] in {{gender:their|his}} evil.
en.B: In my brief life, which is only a breath, I have seen it all: there are righteous people who perish in spite of their righteousness, and there are wicked people who live long in spite of their evil.
en.R: My life passes like a breath, and in it I have seen all kinds of things. I have seen good people die even though they do what is right. And I have seen wicked people live a long time even though they do evil.

decisions.choice: the days of my breath: my brief life
decisions.reason: The phrase is like "the days of his life of breath" in 6:12 (*hevel*, see 1:2). Here the sense leans to brevity: Qoheleth's own life is short.

decisions.choice: in his righteousness ... in his evil: while being righteous, in spite of it
decisions.reason: The small word "in" can mean "in spite of" or "while" (Deuteronomy 1:32). The point is that righteousness does not protect the righteous from death, and wickedness does not cut the wicked off.

decisions.choice: the righteous perish and the wicked live long: what Qoheleth has seen against what is usually taught
decisions.reason: Proverbs teaches that the fear of the LORD lengthens life and the years of the wicked are cut short (Proverbs 10:27). Qoheleth reports cases where it is otherwise (8:14). The book does not resolve the tension.

decisions.choice: prolonging: living long
decisions.reason: The verb means to make long; with "days" understood it means to live long (8:12-13).

decisions.choice: the days of my breath (L); my brief life, which is only a breath (B); my life passes like a breath (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide wording for *hevel* keeps the picture of breath (see 1:2), and Balanced and Readable say the sense it has here (m1).

decisions.choice: good people ... wicked people
decisions.reason: Readable says "good people" and "do what is right" for "righteous", a word many young readers do not use.

source.text: אַל־תְּהִ֤י צַדִּיק֙ הַרְבֵּ֔ה וְאַל־תִּתְחַכַּ֖ם יוֹתֵ֑ר לָ֖מָּה תִּשּׁוֹמֵֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: Do not be righteous much, and do not make yourself wise excessively; why should you ruin yourself?

en.L: Do not be righteous [too] much, and do not make yourself wise excessively; why should you ruin yourself?
en.B: Do not be too righteous, and do not make yourself too wise. Why destroy yourself?
en.R: Do not try too hard to be good, and do not try to be too wise. Why ruin yourself?

decisions.choice: do not be too righteous: a warning against relying on one's own goodness and wisdom
alternatives: a warning against strictness and self-righteousness
advice to be only moderately good
decisions.reason: After verse 15 the warning means that being righteous and wise does not guarantee long life, so do not stake everything on them. Some read it as a warning against self-righteousness or against trying to seem wiser than one is ("make yourself wise"). It is not advice to be a little wicked: verse 17 warns against wickedness too, and verse 18 points to the fear of God. Readers differ on the exact sense.

decisions.choice: ruin yourself: bring yourself to ruin
decisions.reason: The verb can mean to be desolate, to be ruined, or to be stunned with horror. Set beside "why should you die" in verse 17, it most likely means destroying oneself.

decisions.choice: try too hard to be good
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the warning as a matter of overdoing it, which suits both readings in m1.

source.text: אַל־תִּרְשַׁ֥ע הַרְבֵּ֖ה וְאַל־תְּהִ֣י סָכָ֑ל לָ֥מָּה תָמ֖וּת בְּלֹ֥א עִתֶּֽךָ׃

records.literal_gloss: Do not be wicked much, and do not be [a] fool; why should you die in not your time?

en.L: Do not be wicked [too] much, and do not be a fool; why should you die [when it is] not your time?
en.B: Do not be too wicked, and do not be a fool. Why die before your time?
en.R: Do not be very wicked, and do not be a foolish person. Why die before your time?

decisions.choice: do not be too wicked: a warning, not a permission
decisions.reason: The words match verse 16. They do not mean that a little wickedness is acceptable; 7:20 says that no one is without sin, and verse 18 points to the fear of God. The pair warns against both extremes, and against thinking that since the righteous die anyway, wickedness costs nothing.

decisions.choice: a fool: a person who lacks sense
decisions.reason: This is a different word from verse 4 (*sakal*, as in 2:19 and 10:3). It is the person without good sense.

decisions.choice: in not your time: before your time
decisions.reason: To die "not in one's time" is to die early, before life has run its course (Job 22:16).

decisions.choice: a foolish person
decisions.reason: Readable uses the same wording as for *kesil*, since the two words mean much the same here.

source.text: ט֚וֹב אֲשֶׁ֣ר תֶּאֱחֹ֣ז בָּזֶ֔ה וְגַם־מִזֶּ֖ה אַל־תַּנַּ֣ח אֶת־יָדֶ֑ךָ כִּֽי־יְרֵ֥א אֱלֹהִ֖ים יֵצֵ֥א אֶת־כֻּלָּֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: Good that you grasp this, and also from this do not let go your hand; for [one] fearing God will go out [with] all of them.

en.L: [It is] good that you take hold of this one, and also from that one do not let go your hand; for [one who] fears God will come out with all of them.
en.B: It is good to hold on to the one and not to let go of the other, for whoever fears God will come through with both.
en.R: It is good to hold on to one of these warnings and not let go of the other. People who honor God with awe will come through all of this.

decisions.choice: this one ... that one: the two warnings of verses 16 and 17
decisions.reason: "This" and "that" most likely point to the two warnings just given. Hold both: do not trust in your own goodness, and do not give way to wickedness.

decisions.choice: will come out with all of them: will come through both and do justice to both
decisions.reason: The phrase "go out with" is unusual. It may mean to fulfill both warnings, to escape the dangers of both, or to come safely through them all. The general sense is that the fear of God keeps a person from the ruin of either extreme.

decisions.choice: fears God: lives in reverent awe of God
decisions.reason: The book's answer to what it cannot explain (see 3:14 and the main note there; 8:12-13; 12:13).

decisions.choice: honor God with awe
decisions.reason: The book-wide wording for "fear God" at Readable (see 3:14), as Proverbs 1:7 has it for the fear of the LORD.

decisions.choice: both (B); all of this (R)
decisions.reason: "All of them" refers to two things, so Balanced says "both". Readable says "all of this" to keep the phrase open, as m2 is uncertain.

source.text: הַֽחָכְמָ֖ה תָּעֹ֣ז לֶחָכָ֑ם מֵֽעֲשָׂרָה֙ שַׁלִּיטִ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר הָי֖וּ בָּעִֽיר׃

records.literal_gloss: The wisdom makes strong to the wise more than ten rulers who are in the city.

en.L: Wisdom makes the wise [one] strong more than ten rulers who are in the city.
en.B: Wisdom makes a wise person stronger than ten rulers in a city.
en.R: Wisdom makes a wise person stronger than ten rulers of a city.

decisions.choice: ten rulers in a city: a city's leading men, its whole council
decisions.reason: Ten is a round number for a full group (Genesis 18:32; Ruth 4:2). A city was run by its elders and powerful men. One wise person has more strength than all of them together (9:13-18).

decisions.choice: makes strong: gives strength
decisions.reason: The verb means to be or make strong. Wisdom is a kind of power (Proverbs 21:22; 24:5).

source.text: כִּ֣י אָדָ֔ם אֵ֥ין צַדִּ֖יק בָּאָ֑רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֥ר יַעֲשֶׂה־טּ֖וֹב וְלֹ֥א יֶחֱטָֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: For [a] human there is not righteous in the earth who does good and does not sin.

en.L: For [there is] no righteous {{gender:person|man}} on the earth who does good and does not sin.
en.B: Indeed, there is no one on earth so righteous that they always do good and never sin.
en.R: There is no one on earth who always does what is right and never sins.

decisions.choice: no one who does not sin: as Solomon's prayer says
decisions.reason: Solomon's prayer at the temple says the same: "there is no one who does not sin" (1 Kings 8:46). See also Psalm 143:2 and Proverbs 20:9.

decisions.choice: for: the verse explains verses 16-18
decisions.reason: The verse gives the reason for the warnings: no one is so righteous that they can trust in their own righteousness (verse 16). It also leads into verses 21-22, where everyone has cursed someone.

decisions.choice: no one
decisions.reason: The word means a human being, man or woman. Balanced and Readable say "no one"; Literal keeps "person" with the gender setting.

source.text: גַּ֤ם לְכָל־הַדְּבָרִים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר יְדַבֵּ֔רוּ אַל־תִּתֵּ֖ן לִבֶּ֑ךָ אֲשֶׁ֥ר לֹֽא־תִשְׁמַ֥ע אֶֽת־עַבְדְּךָ֖ מְקַלְלֶֽךָ׃

records.literal_gloss: Also to all the words which they speak do not give your heart, so that you will not hear your slave cursing you.

en.L: Also, to all the words that they speak do not give your heart, so that you may not hear your slave cursing you.
en.B: Also, do not take to heart everything people say, or you may hear your servant cursing you.
en.R: Do not pay attention to everything people say. If you do, you may hear your own servant cursing you.

decisions.choice: do not give your heart to: do not pay attention to
decisions.reason: To give the heart to something is to attend to it (verse 2; 1:13). Here it means listening for what everyone says about you.

decisions.choice: your slave: a servant owned by the household
decisions.reason: The word (*'eved*) means a slave or servant, a member of the household who belonged to the master and was not hired. Such a servant would be close enough to overhear and to speak against the master.

decisions.choice: so that you may not hear: if you listen to everything, you will hear your own servant
decisions.reason: The words give the reason for the advice. Whoever listens for every word will hear something painful, even from those closest to them.

decisions.choice: slave (L); servant (B, R)
decisions.reason: The project's wording for *'eved*: "slave" at Literal, "servant" at Balanced and Readable, with the meaning decision (m2) keeping the position the word describes.

decisions.choice: people
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say who "they" are: people in general.

source.text: כִּ֛י גַּם־פְּעָמִ֥ים רַבּ֖וֹת יָדַ֣ע לִבֶּ֑ךָ אֲשֶׁ֥ר גַּם־אַתָּ֖ה קִלַּ֥לְתָּ אֲחֵרִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: For also times many knows your heart that also you have cursed others.

en.L: For your heart knows that many times you too have cursed others.
en.B: For you know in your heart that you yourself have often cursed others.
en.R: You know that many times you yourself have cursed other people.

decisions.choice: your heart knows: you know inside yourself
decisions.reason: The heart knows what a person may not admit aloud. Qoheleth appeals to the reader's conscience.

decisions.choice: you too have cursed others: the reader is no better than the servant
decisions.reason: This links back to verse 20: no one is without sin. The reader who is hurt by the servant's words has said the same about others.

source.text: כָּל־זֹ֖ה נִסִּ֣יתִי בַֽחָכְמָ֑ה אָמַ֣רְתִּי אֶחְכָּ֔מָה וְהִ֖יא רְחוֹקָ֥ה מִמֶּֽנִּי׃

records.literal_gloss: All this I tested by the wisdom; I said, I will be wise, but it [was] far from me.

en.L: All this I tested by wisdom; I said, "I will become wise," but it [was] far from me.
en.B: All this I have tested by wisdom. I said, "I will be wise," but wisdom was far from me.
en.R: I used wisdom to test all of this. I said, "I will become wise." But wisdom was far out of my reach.

decisions.choice: all this: what Qoheleth has said so far, at least in this chapter
decisions.reason: "All this" points back to the sayings and reflections of the chapter, which Qoheleth has tested by wisdom, as he did in 1:13 and 2:3.

decisions.choice: it was far from me: wisdom itself was out of reach
alternatives: what I sought was far off
decisions.reason: "It" is feminine, like the word for wisdom, so the likeliest sense is that wisdom stayed beyond Qoheleth's grasp. Even the wisest cannot master it (8:17).

decisions.choice: double quotation marks for what Qoheleth said to himself
decisions.reason: Words Qoheleth quotes inside his own speech take double quotation marks, as in 1:16 and 2:1.

decisions.choice: wisdom
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name what "it" refers to (m2).

source.text: רָח֖וֹק מַה־שֶּׁהָיָ֑ה וְעָמֹ֥ק׀עָמֹ֖ק מִ֥י יִמְצָאֶֽנּוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: Far [is] what has been, and deep, deep; who can find it?

en.L: Far off [is] what has been, and deep, deep; who can find it out?
en.B: What exists is far off and very deep. Who can find it out?
en.R: What happens in this world is far away from us, and it is very deep. Who can understand it?

decisions.choice: what has been: what exists and happens, the way things are
alternatives: what has happened in the past
decisions.reason: The phrase is the one used in 1:9, 3:15 and 6:10 for what is and has been. Here it is the whole of reality, which wisdom tries to understand.

decisions.choice: deep, deep: very deep
decisions.reason: Repeating a word makes it stronger. What is deep is hard to understand (Proverbs 20:5; Job 11:8).

decisions.choice: who can find it?: no one can
decisions.reason: The question expects the answer "no one" (8:17).

decisions.choice: what happens in this world
decisions.reason: Readable says what the phrase refers to (m1).

source.text: סַבּ֨וֹתִֽי אֲנִ֤י וְלִבִּי֙ לָדַ֣עַת וְלָת֔וּר וּבַקֵּ֥שׁ חָכְמָ֖ה וְחֶשְׁבּ֑וֹן וְלָדַ֨עַת֙ רֶ֣שַׁע כֶּ֔סֶל וְהַסִּכְל֖וּת הוֹלֵלֽוֹת׃

records.literal_gloss: Turned I and my heart to know and to search and to seek wisdom and [an] account, and to know wickedness [as] folly, and the foolishness [as] madness.

en.L: I turned, I and my heart, to know and to explore and to seek wisdom and an accounting, and to know wickedness [as] folly, and foolishness [as] madness.
en.B: I turned my mind to understand, to explore, and to search out wisdom and the reason of things, and to understand that wickedness is folly and foolishness is madness.
en.R: I set my mind to learn, to study and to search for wisdom and for the reason behind things. I wanted to understand that doing evil is foolish, and that foolishness is a kind of madness.

decisions.choice: I turned, I and my heart: I set my whole mind
decisions.reason: Qoheleth often speaks of his heart as a partner in his search (1:13, 16-17; 2:3). The heart is the mind and will.

decisions.choice: accounting: the sum of things, the reckoning that explains them
decisions.reason: The word (*cheshbon*) is a reckoning, a total arrived at by counting (verse 27; 9:10). Qoheleth wants to add things up and understand them. The related word in verse 29 is "schemes".

decisions.choice: to know wickedness as folly and foolishness as madness
alternatives: to know the wickedness of folly, and foolishness that is madness
decisions.reason: The Hebrew sets four nouns side by side. The likeliest sense is that Qoheleth wanted to know that wickedness is folly, and foolishness is madness. Some read: "to know the wickedness of folly and the madness of foolishness". The sense is close either way.

decisions.choice: my mind
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "my mind" for the idiom (m1); Literal keeps the Hebrew.

decisions.choice: the reason of things (B); the reason behind things (R)
decisions.reason: "Accounting" sounds like bookkeeping in everyday speech. Balanced and Readable say what Qoheleth wanted to work out (m2).

source.text: וּמוֹצֶ֨א אֲנִ֜י מַ֣ר מִמָּ֗וֶת אֶת־הָֽאִשָּׁה֙ אֲשֶׁר־הִ֨יא מְצוֹדִ֧ים וַחֲרָמִ֛ים לִבָּ֖הּ אֲסוּרִ֣ים יָדֶ֑יהָ ט֞וֹב לִפְנֵ֤י הָאֱלֹהִים֙ יִמָּלֵ֣ט מִמֶּ֔נָּה וְחוֹטֵ֖א יִלָּ֥כֶד בָּֽהּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And finding I [something] bitter more than the death: the woman who she [is] snares, and nets her heart, chains her hands; [one] good before the God will escape from her, but [one] sinning will be captured by her.

en.L: And I find more bitter than death the woman who [is] snares, and her heart [is] nets, her hands [are] chains; [one who is] good before God will escape from her, but one who sins will be captured by her.
en.B: I find something more bitter than death: the woman who is a trap, whose heart is a net and whose hands are chains. Whoever pleases God will escape her, but the sinner will be caught by her.
en.R: I found something more bitter than death: a woman who is like a hunter's trap. Her heart is like a net, and her hands are like chains. People who please God will get away from her, but sinners will be caught by her.

decisions.choice: the woman who is snares: the seductive woman, the trap that Proverbs warns against
decisions.reason: The woman described is one whose heart is a net and whose hands are chains: one who sets out to trap. This is the seductive woman of Proverbs, whose end is bitter (Proverbs 5:3-5; 7:21-23), who may also stand for folly itself (Proverbs 9:13-18). Some read the verse as a judgment on women in general. That fits poorly with 9:9, where Qoheleth tells his reader to enjoy life with the wife he loves, but the words of verse 28 keep the question open.

decisions.choice: snares, nets, chains: the gear of hunters and jailers
decisions.reason: Snares and nets caught birds and animals (9:12); chains held prisoners. The pictures say that she captures those who come near her.

decisions.choice: good before God: pleasing to God
decisions.reason: The same phrase is used in 2:26 for the one who pleases God, set against the sinner, as here.

decisions.choice: more bitter than death
decisions.reason: Proverbs 5:4 says that the end of the forbidden woman is bitter as wormwood, and her steps lead down to death.

decisions.choice: like a hunter's trap ... like a net ... like chains
decisions.reason: Readable adds "like" so that the metaphors read as pictures, and "a hunter's" to say what kind of trap is meant (m2).

source.text: רְאֵה֙ זֶ֣ה מָצָ֔אתִי אָמְרָ֖ה קֹהֶ֑לֶת אַחַ֥ת לְאַחַ֖ת לִמְצֹ֥א חֶשְׁבּֽוֹן׃

records.literal_gloss: See, this I have found, says Qoheleth, one to one to find [the] sum,

en.L: See, this I have found, says Qoheleth, [adding] one to one to find the sum,
en.B: Look, this is what I have found, says the Teacher, adding one thing to another to find the sum,
en.R: Look, here is what I found, says the Teacher. I put one thing with another to find out how it all adds up.

decisions.choice: says Qoheleth: the voice of the book's frame breaks into Qoheleth's own words
decisions.reason: Qoheleth speaks in the first person from 1:12 to 12:7. Only here, in the middle of that speech, is he named in the third person. The words recall the frame of the book, which speaks about him in 1:1-2 and 12:8-14, and remind the reader that someone else is presenting his words.

decisions.choice: says Qoheleth, read with the consonants divided as in 12:8
alternatives: says she, Qoheleth (with a feminine verb)
decisions.reason: As the Hebrew text is written, the verb "says" is feminine, though everywhere else Qoheleth takes masculine verbs. If the same letters are divided differently, they read "says the Qoheleth", exactly as in 12:8. Some keep the feminine and explain it by the form of the name, which is feminine in shape. The sense is the same either way.

decisions.choice: one to one to find the sum: adding up one thing after another
decisions.reason: The word for "sum" (*cheshbon*) is the reckoning of verse 25. Qoheleth counts up his findings one by one, hoping to reach a total.

decisions.choice: the sentence goes on into verse 28
decisions.reason: What Qoheleth found, and what he did not, follows in verse 28.

decisions.choice: Qoheleth (L); the Teacher (B, R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide wording for *qohelet* (see 1:1). No quotation marks are used: "says Qoheleth" interrupts his own words, as the frame of the book does in 1:2 and 12:8.

decisions.choice: a full stop at the end of the verse
decisions.reason: Readable ends the sentence here and starts verse 28 as a new sentence. Literal and Balanced end with a comma, as the sentence continues.

source.text: אֲשֶׁ֛ר עוֹד־בִּקְשָׁ֥ה נַפְשִׁ֖י וְלֹ֣א מָצָ֑אתִי אָדָ֞ם אֶחָ֤ד מֵאֶ֨לֶף֙ מָצָ֔אתִי וְאִשָּׁ֥ה בְכָל־אֵ֖לֶּה לֹ֥א מָצָֽאתִי׃

records.literal_gloss: which still has sought my soul, but not I have found: [a] man one from [a] thousand I have found, but [a] woman among all these not I have found.

en.L: which my soul has still sought, but I have not found: one man among a thousand I have found, but a woman among all these I have not found.
en.B: which I have kept searching for but have not found. One man among a thousand I have found, but a woman among all these I have not found.
en.R: I kept looking for it, but I did not find it. I found one man among a thousand, but among all of them I did not find one woman.

decisions.choice: my soul has sought: I myself have searched, with longing
decisions.reason: The soul (*nefesh*) is the whole self, with its desires. Qoheleth searched with all his being.

decisions.choice: man ... woman: here the word for a human being is set against the word for a woman, so it means a man
alternatives: one human being among a thousand
decisions.reason: The word (*'adam*) usually means a human being. Here it stands opposite "a woman", so it means a man.

decisions.choice: one man in a thousand, but no woman: what Qoheleth found is not said, and the saying is hard
alternatives: a bitter judgment on women in general
a saying Qoheleth quotes and then corrects in verse 29
about finding a trustworthy person, as Proverbs 20:6
decisions.reason: Qoheleth does not say what he was looking for. It may be the "sum" of verse 27, a person who is truly upright (verse 29), or a trustworthy friend (Proverbs 20:6). Finding one man in a thousand is itself almost nothing. Some read the line as a harsh view of women, others as a common saying that Qoheleth sets up only to correct it in verse 29, where God made all humankind upright and all have gone astray. The Hebrew does not settle the question.

decisions.choice: One man among a thousand I have found
alternatives: I have found one man among a thousand
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the Hebrew order, which sets the two findings side by side for contrast. Readable uses the usual order.

source.text: לְבַד֙ רְאֵה־זֶ֣ה מָצָ֔אתִי אֲשֶׁ֨ר עָשָׂ֧ה הָאֱלֹהִ֛ים אֶת־הָאָדָ֖ם יָשָׁ֑ר וְהֵ֥מָּה בִקְשׁ֖וּ חִשְּׁבֹנ֥וֹת רַבִּֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: Only see this I have found: that made the God the human upright, but they have sought schemes many.

en.L: Only see, this I have found: that God made {{gender:humankind|man}} upright, but they have sought out many schemes.
en.B: This alone I have found: God made {{gender:human beings|mankind}} upright, but they have gone looking for many schemes.
en.R: But here is one thing I have learned: God made people upright, but they have come up with many clever ways to go wrong.

decisions.choice: God made humankind upright: an echo of creation
decisions.reason: The words recall Genesis 1:26-31, where God made humankind and saw that it was very good, and Genesis 3, where the first humans looked for more than they were given.

decisions.choice: humankind ... they: all people, men and women
decisions.reason: The word with the article (*ha'adam*) here means humankind as a whole, and "they" refers to all people. After verse 28, Qoheleth's one firm finding is about everyone, not one sex.

decisions.choice: schemes: clever plans and inventions
decisions.reason: The word (*chishshevonot*) comes from the same root as "sum" in verses 25 and 27. Qoheleth looked for the one true reckoning; people have devised many reckonings of their own. Elsewhere the word is used for clever inventions (2 Chronicles 26:15).

decisions.choice: upright: straight, honest, as people should be
decisions.reason: The word means straight or level, and so honest and right (Psalm 25:8; Proverbs 2:7). It is the opposite of the crooked of verse 13.

decisions.choice: many clever ways to go wrong
decisions.reason: Readable says what kind of schemes are meant, set against "upright". It is a little fuller than the Hebrew, which says only "many schemes".
